opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think prompt engineering can help at the margins, but I'm fairly skeptical that it's a real solution to the hallucination problem. The fundamental issue is that these models are trained to produce plausible continuations of text. They're statistical models of language, not models of the world, and they don't have a clear internal representation of what they know versus what they don't know. So when you ask them a question, they'll give you something that sounds right whether or not it's grounded in any actual fact.

Now, there are prompting strategies that seem to reduce the error rate. You can ask the model to reason step by step, you can tell it to say "I don't know" if it isn't sure, you can give it retrieved documents and instruct it to answer only from those sources. Retrieval augmentation in particular does help, because you're supplying the relevant knowledge in the context rather than relying on whatever got baked into the weights. But even then, the models will sometimes blend the retrieved content with things they've made up, or misattribute claims to the sources.

What concerns me is that prompt engineering is a very brittle, trial-and-error activity. You find a prompt that works on some set of examples, but you have no guarantee it will generalize, and a small change in wording can change the behavior substantially. From an engineering point of view, that's not the kind of reliability we'd want if we're going to deploy these systems in high-stakes settings.

I think the more promising directions are architectural. We need systems that separate the linguistic competence of the language model from the knowledge itself, so that facts live in something like a knowledge base that can be checked, updated, and attributed. And we need much better uncertainty quantification, so that the system can tell us when it's on solid ground and when it's guessing. That's an area I've worked on for a long time, and I think it's essential here. So prompt engineering is a useful tool for practitioners today, but I don't think it's where the long-term answer lies.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'm fairly skeptical that prompt engineering is going to be the answer to hallucinations. It's useful as a tool, don't get me wrong. If you tell the model "only answer based on the following document, and if the answer isn't in the document, say you don't know," you do get fewer fabrications. Techniques like chain-of-thought prompting, or asking the model to cite its sources, help at the margins too. But I think of these as band-aids, because they don't touch the underlying cause of the problem.

The underlying cause is architectural. A large language model is trained to produce plausible continuations of text. It has no explicit representation of what it knows versus what it doesn't know. It doesn't have a separate knowledge base that it consults and then reports on. The "knowledge" is all smeared across the weights, tangled up with the language ability, the stylistic patterns, everything. So when you ask it a factual question, it isn't retrieving a fact, it's generating something that looks like an answer to that kind of question. Sometimes that's correct because the fact appeared many times in training. Sometimes it's a confabulation that has exactly the same surface form. And critically, the model itself can't reliably tell the difference, so no prompt is going to make it tell the difference for you.

There's also a deeper issue, which is that a prompt is just more text in the context. The model is still doing the same computation. You can shift the distribution of its outputs, but you can't make it do something it has no mechanism for doing. If I tell a person "be careful not to make things up," that works because the person has some metacognitive access to their own confidence. The model has something that vaguely resembles that, you can ask it to rate its confidence, but the calibration is often poor, and it's quite sensitive to how you ask.

So where do I think the real progress will come from? I'd point to a few directions. One is retrieval-augmented approaches, where the language model is really serving as an interface to an external, verifiable knowledge source rather than as the knowledge source itself. Then you can audit what it was looking at. Another is architectures that separate the linguistic competence from the world knowledge, so that knowledge can be updated, inspected, and attributed. And a third is better methods for the model to estimate its own uncertainty, which is really an open research problem, and one I care a lot about given my background in anomaly detection and open-category learning. Knowing what you don't know is, in my view, a core requirement for any system we want to call trustworthy.

So, short version: prompt engineering helps, use it, but don't mistake it for a solution. If we want systems that don't hallucinate, we're going to have to change the systems, not just the questions we ask them.

astra-6.text:
I think prompt engineering can help, but I don’t think it’s going to solve the problem by itself. You can ask the model to be careful, to explain its reasoning, or to say when it doesn’t know. But that doesn’t necessarily mean it can distinguish what it knows from what it’s making up. An explanation can be just as plausible—and just as wrong—as the original answer.

A more promising approach is to ground the response in information that we can check. Give the model relevant documents, ask it to answer from those documents, and then verify that the documents actually support the claims it makes. Prompting is useful as part of that process, but it isn’t a guarantee.

The key question is how we establish that an answer is correct. If we simply ask the same model, “Are you sure?” we haven’t introduced much independent evidence. For applications where mistakes matter, we need verification outside the model, and we need a way for the system to abstain when it can’t support an answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think prompt engineering can help, but I don’t see it as a complete solution. You can ask the model to be careful, to explain its assumptions, or to say when it doesn’t know. The difficulty is that asking it to do those things doesn’t establish that it can reliably distinguish what it knows from what it’s making up. It can produce a very convincing explanation for an incorrect answer.

So I would want to separate improving the model’s behavior from verifying its answers. Prompts may improve behavior, but if correctness matters, we need some independent way to check the claims—against documents, a database, or a tool that can actually perform the calculation. And we need to measure how often those checks fail, too. A more reassuring answer isn’t necessarily a more reliable answer.
